content: The Association of State and Territorial Health Officials (ASTHO) conducted a comprehensive survey to evaluate the efforts of state health departments in preventing and controlling tobacco use. This survey provided detailed insights into the components of state tobacco control programs, including budgets, planning, coalitions, surveillance systems, smoking cessation programs, educational activities, legislative actions, and health department policies. The findings revealed significant variability in the strength and scope of these programs across states. The data collected from this survey can be utilized to plan and assess state-level public health initiatives aimed at reducing tobacco-related chronic diseases. Outcomes of these activities can be evaluated using tools such as the CDC's Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS) and the U.S. Census Bureau's Current Population Survey (CPS). In October 1989, ASTHO conducted this survey to assess the progress of states in implementing public health practices to prevent and control tobacco use. The survey also aimed to encourage states to develop and implement tobacco control initiatives. It covered various critical areas, including adult and adolescent tobacco-use surveillance, regulatory activities, coalitions, special populations, community education, economic incentives, and policies in educational institutions. ASTHO established a network of health professionals to facilitate communication between federal and state health departments on tobacco-related issues. These professionals served as the primary respondents for the survey. The survey was divided into ten major sections, addressing topics such as background information on tobacco control, surveillance of adult and adolescent tobacco use, data analysis on tobacco-related diseases, regulatory activities, coalitions, special populations, community education, economic incentives, and policies in educational institutions. State departments of education were involved in answering questions related to tobacco control activities in schools. Supplemental data sources, such as legislative records, taxation data, and school statistics, were used to enhance the survey findings. The survey was distributed to all 50 states and the District of Columbia, achieving a 100% response rate. Data were analyzed using specialized software, and the results highlighted the variability in state-level tobacco control efforts. As of October 1990, 12 states had developed standalone plans for tobacco control, while 22 states included tobacco control as part of broader chronic disease prevention plans. The average state budget for tobacco-related health activities, excluding California, was $70,917, with significant disparities in funding across states. California allocated $151 million, funded by a portion of its cigarette excise tax, while 27 states reported no dedicated funding. Surveillance of adult tobacco use was primarily conducted through the CDC's BRFSS, with 46 states participating in 1990. Additionally, 21 states collected data on adult smoking prevalence from other sources, focusing on specific populations such as racial and ethnic minorities, individuals with low socioeconomic status, and women of reproductive age. For youth tobacco use, no national system existed, but the CDC's Youth Risk Behavior Survey (YRBS) provided a standardized tool for data collection. By the end of 1990, 22 states had participated in the YRBS or similar surveys, collecting data on tobacco experimentation, current use, age of initiation, and smokeless tobacco use. All 51 state health departments used the Smoking-Attributable Mortality, Morbidity, and Economic Costs (SAMMEC) software to estimate smoking-related deaths and economic costs. Some states also recorded smoking history on death certificates and collected data on smoking-attributable hospital discharges and maternal smoking history. In 1989, 45 states had laws restricting smoking in public places, with varying levels of enforcement in workplaces and other settings. Local ordinances further regulated smoking in public spaces such as restaurants, libraries, and public transit. Most state health departments had written policies on smoking in their buildings, with 24 states implementing complete bans. As of October 1990, 46 states prohibited the sale of tobacco products to minors, with minimum age requirements ranging from 16 to 19 years. Nine states restricted tobacco vending machines, and 22 states required retail tobacco licenses for vendors. Two states, Massachusetts and Utah, restricted tobacco advertising on state property, while six states had local policies limiting advertising on government property. Tobacco-control coalitions were active in all 50 states, involving health professionals, community members, policymakers, and educators. These coalitions focused on public education, legislative efforts, professional training, and research. Special populations, including adolescents, women of reproductive age, and racial and ethnic minorities, were targeted for intensive tobacco prevention and control programs. Public information campaigns were conducted in 45 states, utilizing various media to raise awareness about tobacco use. Smoking cessation programs were offered to state employees in 35 states and to the general public in 26 states. Economic incentives, such as differential health insurance rates for smokers and nonsmokers, were implemented in a few states. State excise taxes on cigarettes varied widely, with an average of 23 cents per pack. In educational institutions, 39 states had laws restricting tobacco use in schools, with varying levels of enforcement for students and staff. Tobacco-use prevention education was provided in the majority of public primary and secondary schools, but data on private schools were limited. Approximately 48.5% of students in reporting states attended smoke-free schools. The 1989 ASTHO survey provided a baseline for monitoring state-level tobacco control efforts. Future surveys could assess the impact of intervention programs and guide states toward achieving national health objectives, such as those outlined in Healthy People 2000. These objectives include reducing smoking prevalence, increasing cessation rates, and creating tobacco-free environments in schools and workplaces.
